learningObjective: Explain Halide's separation of algorithm (compute) from schedule and why the design choice matters for performance portability.

canonicalClaims.claim: Halide separates the algorithm (pure functional description of what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute — loop order, tiling, storage, parallelism) because a single algorithm admits many valid schedules with vastly different performance across hardware; the separation allows exploration and portability without endangering correctness.
conditions: The algorithm is expressible in Halide's DSL (or an equivalent tensor-expression language).
The schedule primitives satisfy their legality preconditions.
nonImplications: Does not imply any schedule is valid; schedule primitives have preconditions.
Does not imply schedule search is trivial; autoschedulers can spend significant time.

misconceptions.claim: The algorithm / schedule split in Halide is primarily for compile-time type checking.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Type checking is orthogonal; the split is about performance exploration and portability.

misconceptions.claim: One Halide schedule can be reused across multiple algorithms.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Schedules are indexed by the algorithm's Funcs; they are algorithm-specific.

misconceptions.claim: Schedules in Halide are interpreted at runtime while algorithms are compiled.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both are compiled together into the target lowering; there is no runtime schedule interpreter.

misconceptions.claim: The Halide split makes performance tuning irrelevant since any schedule yields the same performance.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The split enables tuning by making it easy — it does not eliminate the tuning problem.

implementationFacts: Halide's schedule primitives include split, tile, reorder, vectorize, unroll, parallel, compute_at, store_at.
TVM's TE and TensorIR schedules follow the same algorithm-schedule split.
performanceScenarios: A stencil algorithm gets 3× speedup by switching from row-major to blocked schedule on the same CPU.
